Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents

shortlist.raw_text: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

shortlist.raw_text: Models for physical AI tasks, such as robotics and autonomous driving, need not reason solely in language. They can use visual plans--points, bounding boxes, and trajectories--to represent spatial goals and anticipate motion. However, autoregressive vision-language models generate these plans one coordinate token at a time, making richer predictions increasingly costly. We introduce VFlash, a method for fast, accurate visual planning through Flash Primitive Decoding. VFlash exploits the known structure of visual primitives to predict their coordinates jointly, using a lightweight drafter that generates an entire primitive in one forward pass. The layout adapts to the primitive's type, dimensionality, and length, supporting compact boxes and long, variable-length trajectories. Crucially, spatial accuracy need not require reproducing an autoregressive model's exact token sequence. VFlash therefore trains on annotated primitives and directly accepts structurally valid predictions without target-token agreement. Across the evaluated 2D and 3D robot trajectory tasks, VFlash consistently reduces prediction errors relative to autoregressive decoding. Preliminary single-rollout measurements indicate approximately 25x faster generation for 3D point motion forecasting. A world action model conditioned on VFlash plans achieves 70.2% average success across four MolmoSpaces task suites, compared with 62.6% for the baseline.

shortlist.raw_text: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

shortlist.raw_text: Harness evolution from a common base exhibits Locality, Complementarity, and Nonstationarity: variants repair different failures, and their utility changes as the policy learns. Rather than seeking a universally superior harness, we introduce Harness-S to selectively rescue failures of a base execution system through sibling harnesses and transfer the resulting capabilities into a single policy that remains effective under the original harness. Directional Harness Evolution develops specialized sibling harnesses along distinct repair directions, forming a reusable Sibling Harness Pool that remains fixed during policy training. Complementary Harness Rescue Training invokes this pool only when all initial attempts under the base harness fail. The same policy generates fresh rollouts under selected auxiliary harnesses, and these trajectories replace the failed group for reinforcement learning. An Adaptive Harness Router selects the Top-k variants using Harness Behavior Profiles and voting across multiple LLMs. Policy-aware profile re-anchoring refreshes this evidence as the policy learns. Across AppWorld, SWE-Gym, and DBBench, the trained policy substantially outperforms policy-only training when returned to the original base harness. Behavioral analyses and held-out cases support the transfer of harness-elicited behaviors into the policy itself. Reusing the router for Rank-1 inference provides additional gains at the same executor rollout count.

Article text (excerpt):
The travel company is planning an “AI-native” trip-planning experience that’s set to roll out next year.
The travel company is planning an “AI-native” trip-planning experience that’s set to roll out next year.
Airbnb plans to roll out an AI agent in the first half of 2027 that will help users plan and book travel, the company said in its Q3 2026 earnings shareholder letter released today .
“Today’s AI agents are good at simple, routine tasks, like making a restaurant reservation or scheduling an appointment,” Airbnb said. “But planning a trip on Airbnb is different.” The company argued that its experience matching hosts and guests, its current role in being part of reservations already, and a “new interface” built “specifically for travel” gives it an edge.
Here’s how Airbnb says that new interface will work:
We don’t think a traditional chatbot is the right way to plan a trip. We’re developing a custom-designed, AI-native experience that builds the interface around your question. Rather than a chat window, our agent draws on a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements—maps, photos, comparisons, calendars, itineraries—and composes them in real time to match what you’re looking for. Our agent will help guests explore options, make decisions with the people they’re traveling with, and take action directly in Airbnb.
Airbnb co-founder and CEO Brian Chesky has said before that the company plans to launch an agent in 2027, telling the Skift Global Forum that it would have an interface that’s “much richer than a chatbot.”
In its shareholder letter, Airbnb also said that AI is “the best thing to ever happen to Airbnb” and has changed how it develops products and operates.
This is the title for the native ad
text:
Airbnb is ditching the standard chatbot window for its next AI launch.

In its Q3 2026 shareholder letter, the company announced an AI agent coming in 2027 that builds custom screens on the fly.

Here is how the interface actually works.

Most AI assistants force you into a text box. Airbnb claims trip planning is too complex for basic chat.

Instead of sending back text, the system draws from a library of hundreds of travel-specific interface elements.

It composes those visual elements in real time based on your question:
• Maps placed next to listing photos
• Side-by-side room comparisons
• Live calendars and shared itineraries

You get a layout tailored to your search, letting travel groups compare options and book without leaving the app.

CEO Brian Chesky previously previewed the design at the Skift Global Forum, calling it richer than a traditional chatbot.

In the letter, Airbnb went further, calling AI the best thing to ever happen to the company.

My read: the text prompt is a temporary interface. The real value of AI starts when software generates custom controls for a specific job instead of making you read standard text replies.

Keep in mind: this is an earnings letter promise for the first half of 2027, not a live tool anyone can test today.

Would you trade a chat window for a dynamic interface?

Source: The Verge

Line 1: 2027 is the deadline Airbnb set to replace standard booking screens with AI.
Line 2: Its Q3 2026 shareholder letter outlines an agent that generates visual interfaces on the fly.
Prefer when: your audience cares about corporate timelines and long-term product roadmaps.

2. Your X
Line 1: Your next Airbnb search will not involve typing into a traditional chatbot box.
Line 2: A Q3 2026 shareholder letter reveals an upcoming AI agent that composes customized software layouts as you ask questions.
Prefer when: writing directly to consumer-facing founders or product managers focused on user experience.

3. Story in motion
Line 1: Airbnb just told shareholders that AI is the best thing to ever happen to its business.
Line 2: Its Q3 2026 letter details a plan for 2027 that replaces text responses with dynamically generated visual software.
Prefer when: you want maximum emotional pull from a bold corporate quote right away.

Pick: The primary opening ("Airbnb is ditching the standard chatbot window for its next AI launch."). It states the product change clearly, establishes the mechanism instantly, and challenges the common standard of AI text boxes before the line break.
